## Core Overview
Chapter 4 explores threads as the fundamental unit of CPU utilization. It contrasts single-threaded and multithreaded processes, emphasizing how threads enable concurrency and parallelism in modern multicore architectures to improve application performance, responsiveness, and resource efficiency.

## Key Concepts & Theorems/Formulas
- Thread Components: A thread comprises a thread ID, program counter (PC), register set, and stack. It shares the code section, data section, and OS resources (like files) with other threads in the same process.
- Benefits of Multithreading:
  - Responsiveness: Allows continued execution if part of a process is blocked.
  - Resource Sharing: Threads share memory and resources by default, which is easier than shared memory or message passing.
  - Economy: Thread creation and context switching have lower overhead than process creation.
  - Scalability: Processes can take advantage of multicore architectures.
- Concurrency vs. Parallelism:
  - Concurrency: Supports more than one task making progress (interleaving on a single processor).
  - Parallelism: Implies a system can perform more than one task simultaneously (multiple cores).
- Data vs. Task Parallelism:
  - Data Parallelism: Distributes subsets of the same data across cores; same operation on each.
  - Task Parallelism: Distributes unique threads across cores; each performs a unique operation.
- Amdahl's Law: Identifies performance gains from adding cores to an application with serial and parallel components.
  Formula: speedup <= 1 / (S + (1 - S) / N)
  Where S = serial portion and N = number of processing cores.
- Multithreading Models:
  - Many-to-One: Many user threads map to one kernel thread. A single block stops all threads.
  - One-to-One: Each user thread maps to a kernel thread (Windows, Linux).
  - Many-to-Many: Multiplexes many user threads to a smaller/equal number of kernel threads.
- Thread Cancellation:
  - Asynchronous: Terminates the target thread immediately.
  - Deferred: Target thread periodically checks if it should terminate at "cancellation points."

## Exam Takeaways
- Process vs. Thread: Processes are "heavy-weight" units; threads are "light-weight" units of execution within a process.
- Amdahl's Law Impact: The serial portion (S) of an application limits the maximum speedup regardless of the number of cores. As N approaches infinity, speedup approaches 1/S.
- Linux Implementation: Linux refers to threads as "tasks." The clone() system call creates tasks, using flags to control the level of sharing (e.g., CLONE_FS, CLONE_VM).
- Windows Thread Context: Defined by the register set, stacks (user and kernel), and private storage area. Primary structures include ETHREAD, KTHREAD, and TEB.
- Signal Handling: Signals are used in UNIX to notify processes of events. In multithreading, signals can be delivered to the thread to which it applies, every thread, or a specific designated thread.
